reference.source: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Caused by Bartonella species, principally Bartonella henselae and Bartonella quintana, and characterised by a vasoproliferative response to infection
Occurs predominantly in immunocompromised hosts, especially those with advanced HIV and low CD4 counts, and rarely in immunocompetent individuals
Bartonella henselae is associated with cat and cat-flea exposure, whereas Bartonella quintana is linked to body lice, homelessness and poor hygiene
The hallmark is one or more friable, red to purple vascular papules or nodules that can bleed readily and may resemble pyogenic granuloma or Kaposi sarcoma
Visceral disease includes hepatic and splenic bacillary peliosis, and lesions may also involve bone, causing painful osteolytic lesions, and other organs
Histology of a lesion shows lobular vascular proliferation with clumps of bacilli demonstrable on Warthin-Starry silver staining
Prolonged antimicrobial therapy is required, and the condition responds well, distinguishing it from the Kaposi sarcoma it can mimic clinically
reference.pathophysiology: Bartonella species are fastidious Gram-negative bacteria that, in the susceptible host, invade endothelial cells and stimulate a marked angioproliferative response. Bacterial factors promote endothelial cell proliferation and inhibit apoptosis, generating the characteristic lobular capillary proliferations seen in skin, liver, spleen, bone and other tissues. The impaired cellular immunity of the host permits this proliferative, rather than granulomatous or self-limiting, response, and the resulting friable neovascular lesions account for the bleeding tendency and the peliotic blood-filled spaces in affected viscera.
additionalDifferentials: Cutaneous lymphoma or metastatic vascular tumour
Verruga peruana (Bartonella bacilliformis) in endemic regions
Disseminated fungal infection with cutaneous lesions
additionalInvestigations: Skin or tissue biopsy with Warthin-Starry silver stain demonstrating clustered bacilli
PCR of tissue for Bartonella species
Prolonged-incubation blood cultures where bacteraemia is suspected
HIV testing and CD4 count to assess immune status
Cross-sectional imaging of liver and spleen if visceral peliosis is suspected
redFlags: Hepatosplenic peliosis with abdominal pain, fever or cytopenias
Undiagnosed underlying HIV or other profound immunosuppression
Systemic bacteraemic illness with fever and weight loss
Misidentification as Kaposi sarcoma delaying curative antibiotic therapy
reference.prognosis: Bacillary angiomatosis is a treatable and generally curable infection that responds well to prolonged antibiotics, but untreated visceral or disseminated disease can be life-threatening, and relapse may occur if therapy is too short.
pitfalls: Mistaking lesions for Kaposi sarcoma and missing a treatable infection
Using too short an antibiotic course, leading to relapse
Failing to test for and address underlying immunosuppression
Overlooking visceral or osseous involvement in a patient with cutaneous disease
Not eliciting cat, flea or body-louse exposure that points to the causative species
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
